```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE,
    comment = "#>"

```

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(multigrain)
library(ggplot2)

# Every slow step of this article (simulation, boundary tables, optimisation)
# was run once by data-raw/gsd-joint-spending-vignette.R; the article shows
# the code and prints the stored results.
stored <- readRDS("./data/gsd-joint-spending.rds")
main_base <- stored$main_base
main_joint <- stored$main_joint
ex5_base <- stored$ex5_base
ex5_joint <- stored$ex5_joint
at_m4 <- main_joint$spending_profile[main_joint$spending_profile$value == -4, ]

fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f")
gain_of <- function(res) res$power$trial_success
gamma_of <- function(res) unname(res$spending_param[[1L]])

# the connected run of profile nodes around the chosen value within 5e-4 of
# the maximum, as print() reports it
plateau <- function(res, column = "diff", tol = 5e-4) {
    prof <- res$spending_profile[order(res$spending_profile$value), ]
    gap <- if (column == "diff") {
        prof$diff
    } else {
        max(prof[[column]]) - prof[[column]]
    }
    best <- match(gamma_of(res), prof$value)
    lo <- best
    hi <- best
    while (lo > 1L && gap[lo - 1L] <= tol) lo <- lo - 1L
    while (hi < nrow(prof) && gap[hi + 1L] <= tol) hi <- hi + 1L
    prof$value[c(lo, hi)]
}
```

## What this article covers

A group sequential design (GSD) looks at the data more than once. Each
hypothesis then needs a *spending function*, which decides how much of its
significance level may be used at each look. Spending functions are usually
picked from a short list before the graph is optimised. This article shows how
**`multigrain`** can choose one spending parameter *together with* the graph,
and how to read the result.

It builds on two other articles, which it does not repeat:

- [Getting started](get-started.html) explains graphical multiple testing
  procedures (hypothesis weights $\mathbf{w}$ and transition matrix
  $\mathbf{G}$), gain functions and `graph_optimise()`.
- [Trial success measures](trial_success.html) explains the group sequential
  workflow with *fixed* spending functions: `simulate_pvalues_gsd()`,
  `transform_pvalues_gsd()`, gains that depend on when a hypothesis is
  rejected (`trial_success_gsd()` and its discount tables), stopping rules
  (`stopping_rule_gsd()`) and `graph_optimise_gsd()`.

The optimisation framework is described in [Spiers et al. (2026),
*Gain-function optimisation of graphical multiple testing procedures for
confirmatory clinical trials* (arXiv:2609.19994v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19994).
The second example below extends its Example 5.

## A short primer on interim analyses and spending

**Interim analyses.** In a GSD the data are analysed at planned *looks*, for
example once when half the patients have their outcome and once at the end.
The amount of data at a look is its *information fraction* $t$: $t = 0.5$ at
the halfway look and $t = 1$ at the final one. If a hypothesis is rejected at
an interim look, the trial can stop early for efficacy.

**Spending functions.** Testing the same hypothesis at full level $\alpha$ at
every look would inflate the type I error. Instead, each hypothesis gets an
*α-spending function* $\alpha(t)$: the cumulative part of its level that may be
used by information fraction $t$, rising to the whole level at $t = 1$. The
boundary at each look is set so that the probability of crossing any boundary
by that look, under the null hypothesis, equals $\alpha(t)$. A spending
function that spends little early keeps almost the full level for the final
analysis; one that spends a lot early makes early rejection more likely but
leaves a stricter final boundary.

**The Hwang–Shih–DeCani family.** The HSD spending functions
(`gsDesign::sfHSD()`) have one parameter $\gamma$:

$$
\alpha(t) = \alpha \, \frac{1 - e^{-\gamma t}}{1 - e^{-\gamma}}, \qquad
\gamma \neq 0,
$$

and $\alpha(t) = \alpha t$ for $\gamma = 0$. Some texts write the parameter as
$\theta$. Negative values spend little early: at $t = 0.5$, $\gamma = -4$ has
spent about 12% of the level, close to O'Brien–Fleming spending. $\gamma = 0$
spends in proportion to information, and $\gamma = 1$ has spent about 62% at
$t = 0.5$, close to Pocock spending. So one number moves the design smoothly
between the two textbook choices.

```{r spending-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, out.width='100%'}
alpha <- 0.025
t <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
gammas <- c(-4, -2, 0, 1)

spent <- do.call(rbind, lapply(gammas, function(g) {
    data.frame(
        t = t,
        spent = gsDesign::sfHSD(alpha, t, g)$spend / alpha,
        curve = sprintf("HSD, gamma = %g", g)
    )
}))
spent <- rbind(
    spent,
    data.frame(
        t = t,
        spent = gsDesign::sfLDOF(alpha, t)$spend / alpha,
        curve = "sfLDOF (O'Brien-Fleming type)"
    )
)
spent$curve <- factor(spent$curve, levels = unique(spent$curve))

ggplot(spent, aes(t, spent, colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(rep("solid", 4), "dashed")) +
    labs(
        x = "Information fraction t",
        y = "Proportion of the level spent",
        colour = NULL,
        linetype = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

The dotted line marks the interim look used below. The dashed curve,
`gsDesign::sfLDOF`, is the Lan–DeMets O'Brien–Fleming-type function used for
the primary hypothesis throughout.

## Why spending and graph should be chosen together

Take two hypotheses: a primary $H_1$ and a key secondary $H_2$, each tested at
an interim look ($t = 0.5$) and a final look ($t = 1$), at one-sided
$\alpha = 0.025$. The nominal powers are 0.90 and 0.80 and the test statistics
are correlated with $\rho = 0.5$. $H_1$ uses `gsDesign::sfLDOF`.

The gain values $H_1$ at 0.6 and $H_2$ at 0.4. A claim at the final analysis
is worth 0.8 of the same claim at the interim (the discount table `d`), and
the trial **stops as soon as $H_1$ is rejected**:

```{r design, eval=FALSE}
gain <- trial_success_gsd(0.6 * d(t1) + 0.4 * d(t2), d = c(1, 0.8))
rule <- stopping_rule_gsd(r1)
```

Here `t1` and `t2` are the looks at which $H_1$ and $H_2$ were rejected
(0 if never), and `r1` is "$H_1$ has been rejected"; see
[Trial success measures](trial_success.html) for the syntax.

The stopping rule is what ties the spending of $H_2$ to the graph. If $H_1$
is rejected at the interim, the trial stops there, so $H_2$ gets its interim
look and nothing else. Whether $H_2$ is rejected in that trial then depends on
two things:

1. **How much level the graph gives $H_2$**: its own weight $w_2$, plus what
   $H_1$ passes on once it is rejected.
2. **How much of that level $H_2$'s spending function lets it use at
   $t = 0.5$.** Under O'Brien–Fleming-type spending it is very little.

The graph also decides how often the trial stops: a larger $w_1$ makes an
interim rejection of $H_1$, and therefore a stop, more likely. With
O'Brien–Fleming-type spending on $H_2$ a stop is costly, so the best graph
keeps $w_1$ low. With spending that uses more of the level early, a stop costs
less and the best graph can put more weight on $H_1$. The best graph depends on
the spending function, and the best spending function depends on the graph, so
the two should be chosen together.

## Simulate the p-values once

`simulate_pvalues_gsd()` draws raw p-values at every look; the
information fractions are stored with them.

```{r simulate, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(20261007)
raw <- simulate_pvalues_gsd(
    power_nominal = c(H1 = 0.90, H2 = 0.80),
    corr_matrix = matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), nrow = 2),
    info_frac = c(0.5, 1),
    nsim = 1e5
)
```

Both runs below use these same draws, so their gains can be compared directly.

## Baseline: fixed spending

First, the usual approach: fix the spending of both hypotheses at
`gsDesign::sfLDOF` and optimise the graph alone.

```{r baseline, eval=FALSE}
pv_ldof <- transform_pvalues_gsd(raw, spending = gsDesign::sfLDOF)

main_base <- graph_optimise_gsd(
    pv_ldof,
    graph_constraint_free(2),
    gain,
    stopping_rule = rule
)
main_base
```

```{r baseline-print, echo=FALSE}
main_base
```

## Joint optimisation

To let the spending of $H_2$ be chosen, tag it with `sf_hsd_opt()` in the list
of spending functions. `transform_pvalues_gsd()` then returns a *spending
spec* instead of transformed p-values:

```{r spec, eval=FALSE}
spec <- transform_pvalues_gsd(
    raw,
    spending = list(gsDesign::sfLDOF, sf_hsd_opt())
)
spec
```

```{r spec-print, echo=FALSE}
cat(stored$main_spec_print, sep = "\n")
```

The search does not try every real value of $\gamma$. It tries a *lattice*:
by default $-4$ to $1$ in steps of $0.25$, 21 values (`sf_hsd_opt()` takes
`bounds` and `step` to change it). For each value the spec holds a boundary
table, built and checked when the spec is created; building them is the slow
step, about 20 seconds here. The same spec can be reused with other gains and
stopping rules on the same draws.

Pass the spec to `graph_optimise_gsd()` in place of the p-values:

```{r joint, eval=FALSE}
main_joint <- graph_optimise_gsd(
    spec,
    graph_constraint_free(2),
    gain,
    stopping_rule = rule
)
main_joint
```

```{r joint-print, echo=FALSE}
main_joint
```

The search runs in two stages. A genetic algorithm first searches the graph
and $\gamma$ together. Then, at every lattice value of $\gamma$, the graph is
re-optimised, starting from a neighbouring value's graph. The second stage
gives the *profile*: the best achievable gain at each $\gamma$. The chosen
value is in `main_joint$spending_param` and the profile in
`main_joint$spending_profile`.

## Comparing the two designs

```{r compare-table, echo=FALSE}
design_row <- function(label, res, h2_spending) {
    p <- res$power
    data.frame(
        Design = label,
        `H2 spending` = h2_spending,
        w1 = res$hyp_weight[[1L]],
        w2 = res$hyp_weight[[2L]],
        g12 = res$trans_matrix[1L, 2L],
        g21 = res$trans_matrix[2L, 1L],
        `Power H1` = p$local_power[[1L]],
        `Power H2` = p$local_power[[2L]],
        `H2 at interim` = p$time_distribution[2L, 2L],
        `Mean stop look` = p$mean_stop_look,
        Gain = gain_of(res),
        check.names = FALSE
    )
}
knitr::kable(
    rbind(
        design_row("Fixed spending", main_base, "sfLDOF"),
        design_row("Joint", main_joint, main_joint$spending[[2L]])
    ),
    digits = c(NA, NA, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4)
)
```

`w1`, `w2` are the hypothesis weights and `g12`, `g21` the transition weights
($H_1 \to H_2$ and $H_2 \to H_1$). `Power H1` and `Power H2` are the
probabilities of rejecting each hypothesis at any look, `H2 at interim` the
probability of rejecting $H_2$ at the interim, and `Mean stop look` the
average look at which the trial ends.

```{r compare-graphs, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, out.width='100%'}
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plot(main_base, title = "Fixed spending (sfLDOF)"),
    plot(main_joint, title = "Joint (sfHSD for H2)"),
    ncol = 2
)
```

The optimiser chooses $\gamma^* = `r gamma_of(main_joint)`$ for $H_2$, which
spends much earlier than O'Brien–Fleming, and the gain rises from
`r fmt(gain_of(main_base))` to `r fmt(gain_of(main_joint))`. The graph moves
too: the weight on $H_1$ goes from `r fmt(main_base$hyp_weight[[1L]], 3)` to
`r fmt(main_joint$hyp_weight[[1L]], 3)`. Because $H_2$ can now use more of its
level at the interim, a stop after an interim rejection of $H_1$ costs less,
so the graph can afford to back the primary hypothesis more.

The overall power of $H_2$ falls slightly, from
`r fmt(main_base$power$local_power[[2L]], 3)` to
`r fmt(main_joint$power$local_power[[2L]], 3)`, because spending more early
leaves a stricter final boundary. But $H_2$ is now rejected at the interim
in `r fmt(main_joint$power$time_distribution[2L, 2L], 3)` of trials instead of
`r fmt(main_base$power$time_distribution[2L, 2L], 3)`, and under this gain
and stopping rule an earlier claim is worth more than a slightly likelier late
one.

## Reading the output

**The spending lines in `print()`.** Under `Spending functions:` each
hypothesis has a label. A tagged hypothesis shows the chosen function, here
`sfHSD(param = `r gamma_of(main_joint)`)`, marked `[optimised: ...]` with the
parameter's name (`gamma`, or the `id` given to `sf_hsd_opt()`), its bounds and
its step. The next lines sum up the profile as two *plateaus*, explained below.

**The profile table in `summary()`.** `summary()` prints the graph, the gain,
the power and the constraints, followed by the profile, which is shown here:

```{r summary, eval=FALSE}
summary(main_joint)
```

```{r summary-profile, echo=FALSE}
out <- utils::capture.output(summary(main_joint))
first <- grep("Spending-parameter profile", out, fixed = TRUE)
last <- grep("GA visited", out, fixed = TRUE)
cat(out[first:last], sep = "\n")
```

Each row is one lattice value of $\gamma$:

- `gain`: the best gain at that value, with the graph re-optimised there.
- `gain_fixed_graph`: the gain at that value of the graph chosen overall,
  kept as it is.
- `diff`: how far `gain` falls short of the optimum. Every row is computed on
  the same simulated trials, so the difference is *paired* and much more
  precise than either gain on its own.
- `se`: the standard error of `diff`. It is 0 at the chosen value.
- `n_eval`: the number of gain evaluations the local search used at that
  value.

**Plateaus.** A plateau is the run of $\gamma$ values around the optimum whose
gain is within $5 \times 10^{-4}$ of the best. Inside it the differences are
a few standard errors at most, so the values are as good as each other for
practical purposes. `print()` reports two: one for `gain` (graph re-optimised
at each $\gamma$) and one for `gain_fixed_graph` (graph held at the chosen
one). The plot below draws the `value`, `gain` and `gain_fixed_graph` columns
of `main_joint$spending_profile`:

```{r profile-helper, echo=FALSE}
plot_profile <- function(res) {
    prof <- res$spending_profile
    band <- plateau(res)
    long <- rbind(
        data.frame(value = prof$value, gain = prof$gain,
                   curve = "graph re-optimised (gain)"),
        data.frame(value = prof$value, gain = prof$gain_fixed_graph,
                   curve = "chosen graph kept (gain_fixed_graph)")
    )
    ggplot(long, aes(value, gain, colour = curve)) +
        annotate(
            "rect", xmin = band[1L], xmax = band[2L],
            ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.15
        ) +
        geom_line() +
        geom_point() +
        geom_vline(xintercept = gamma_of(res), linetype = "dotted") +
        labs(x = "gamma", y = "Gain", colour = NULL) +
        theme_minimal() +
        theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

```{r profile-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, out.width='100%'}
plot_profile(main_joint)
```

The shaded band is the plateau of `gain`; the dotted line marks $\gamma^*$.

How to use the plateau when writing a protocol:

- **A wide plateau** means the gain hardly depends on $\gamma$ within that
  range. Pick a round, easily justified value inside it and pre-specify it;
  nothing is lost by not using $\gamma^*$ exactly.
- **A narrow plateau** means $\gamma$ matters. Report the chosen value with
  the graph, and check it on fresh simulations (next section).
- **The fixed-graph plateau narrower than the re-optimised one** means the
  best graph changes with $\gamma$. If you move $\gamma$ within the wider
  plateau, re-optimise the graph at the new value too.
- **An optimum on a bound** of the lattice means the gain may still rise beyond
  it. Widen `bounds` in `sf_hsd_opt()` (from $-10$ up to $2$) and run again.

In this design both plateaus run from $`r plateau(main_joint)[1L]`$ to
$`r plateau(main_joint)[2L]`$. Any $\gamma$ in that range is as good as
$\gamma^*$ to within the simulation error, and since the two plateaus agree,
the best graph barely moves across it. At $\gamma = -4$, close to O'Brien–Fleming, the gain is
`r fmt(at_m4$diff)` lower, about `r round(at_m4$diff / at_m4$se)` standard
errors.

## Checking the chosen design on fresh simulations

The graph and $\gamma$ were chosen on the same simulated trials that score
them, so the reported gain is slightly optimistic (the "winner's curse"). To
check it, simulate new p-values, build a spec from them with the same
spending functions, and use `resolve_pvalues_gsd()` to obtain the transformed
p-values at the chosen $\gamma$. Then evaluate the chosen graph on them:

```{r fresh, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(20261008)
raw_new <- simulate_pvalues_gsd(
    power_nominal = c(H1 = 0.90, H2 = 0.80),
    corr_matrix = matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), nrow = 2),
    info_frac = c(0.5, 1),
    nsim = 1e5
)
spec_new <- transform_pvalues_gsd(
    raw_new,
    spending = list(gsDesign::sfLDOF, sf_hsd_opt())
)
pv_new <- resolve_pvalues_gsd(spec_new, main_joint$spending_param)

check <- calc_power_pvals_gsd(
    pv_new,
    hyp_weight = main_joint$hyp_weight,
    trans_matrix = main_joint$trans_matrix,
    stopping_rule = rule,
    custom_power = list(gain = gain)
)
round(check$gain, 4)
```

```{r fresh-print, echo=FALSE}
round(stored$main_check$gain, 4)
```

On fresh draws the design scores `r fmt(stored$main_check$gain)`, against
`r fmt(gain_of(main_joint))` reported by the optimiser. Only lattice values
can be resolved, because only their boundary tables were built and checked.

## A second example: the paper's Example 5

Example 5 of the paper has two endpoints with different timing.
Progression-free survival (PFS, $H_1$) is complete at the interim analysis:
its information fraction is 1 at both looks, so its spending function has no
effect. Overall survival (OS, $H_2$) has 70% of its information at the interim
and all of it at the final analysis. The nominal powers are 0.98 and 0.93 and
$\rho = 0.5$. PFS is valued at 0.4 and OS at 0.6. A PFS claim made only at the
final analysis keeps half its value, and an OS claim at the final analysis
keeps 75%. There is no stopping rule.

The paper fixes O'Brien–Fleming-type spending for OS. Here we let OS's
spending be chosen with the graph:

```{r ex5, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(20261014)
raw5 <- simulate_pvalues_gsd(
    power_nominal = c(PFS = 0.98, OS = 0.93),
    corr_matrix = matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), nrow = 2),
    info_frac = rbind(PFS = c(1, 1), OS = c(0.7, 1)),
    nsim = 1e5
)
gain5 <- trial_success_gsd(
    0.4 * d_pfs(t1) + 0.6 * d_os(t2),
    d_pfs = c(1, 0.50),
    d_os = c(1, 0.75)
)

# baseline: OS spending fixed at sfLDOF
ex5_base <- graph_optimise_gsd(
    transform_pvalues_gsd(raw5, spending = gsDesign::sfLDOF),
    graph_constraint_free(2),
    gain5
)

# joint: OS tagged
spec5 <- transform_pvalues_gsd(
    raw5,
    spending = list(gsDesign::sfLDOF, sf_hsd_opt())
)
ex5_joint <- graph_optimise_gsd(spec5, graph_constraint_free(2), gain5)
ex5_joint
```

```{r ex5-print, echo=FALSE}
ex5_joint
```

```{r ex5-table, echo=FALSE}
ex5_row <- function(label, res, os_spending) {
    p <- res$power
    data.frame(
        Design = label,
        `OS spending` = os_spending,
        `w PFS` = res$hyp_weight[[1L]],
        `w OS` = res$hyp_weight[[2L]],
        `Power PFS` = p$local_power[[1L]],
        `Power OS` = p$local_power[[2L]],
        `OS at interim` = p$time_distribution[2L, 2L],
        Gain = gain_of(res),
        check.names = FALSE
    )
}
knitr::kable(
    rbind(
        ex5_row("Fixed spending", ex5_base, "sfLDOF"),
        ex5_row("Joint", ex5_joint, ex5_joint$spending[[2L]])
    ),
    digits = c(NA, NA, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4)
)
```

`OS at interim` is the proportion of trials in which OS is rejected at the
interim analysis.

```{r ex5-profile, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, out.width='100%'}
plot_profile(ex5_joint)
```

Even without a stopping rule, the time discount rewards spending earlier
for OS. The optimiser chooses $\gamma^* = `r gamma_of(ex5_joint)`$, OS is
rejected at the interim in `r fmt(ex5_joint$power$time_distribution[2L, 2L], 3)`
of trials instead of `r fmt(ex5_base$power$time_distribution[2L, 2L], 3)`, and
the gain rises from `r fmt(gain_of(ex5_base))` to `r fmt(gain_of(ex5_joint))`.

This example differs from the first in two ways:

- **The graph hardly moves.** The weight on PFS goes from
  `r fmt(ex5_base$hyp_weight[[1L]], 3)` to `r fmt(ex5_joint$hyp_weight[[1L]], 3)`,
  and the two plateaus are the same. Without a stopping rule an interim
  rejection of PFS costs OS nothing, so the coupling between the graph and the
  spending is weak. Here the spending could have been chosen on its own.
- **The plateau is wide**, from $`r plateau(ex5_joint)[1L]`$ to
  $`r plateau(ex5_joint)[2L]`$. Any value in that range, including the
  conventional $\gamma = 0$ (spending in proportion to information), would do.
  Both textbook ends are clearly worse, O'Brien–Fleming-like spending much more
  so than Pocock-like spending.

## Simulation error does not affect error control

Monte Carlo error and the coarseness of the lattice affect only the power and
gain reported for a design, never its familywise error rate: every value of
$\gamma$ the search can choose has a boundary table checked before the search
starts, and the procedure controls the error rate for any fixed choice.

  `resolve_pvalues_gsd()` and `graph_optimise_gsd()`, including how to share
